\begin{bankq}[id=SI01-P2-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 01 (16 Jun 2021)}, paper=2, qno=2, type=single, subtopic={YDSE}, answer={A}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: coincident bright fringes for two wavelengths on a screen | steps: n1 lambda1 = n2 lambda2; minimum distance from centre; lowest integers}]
Coherent light consisting of two wavelengths $\lambda_1=4500$ \AA\ \& $\lambda_2=6000$ \AA\ is sent through both slits of a Young's double slit apparatus (Source is placed symmetrically for both the slits)
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Central maxima for both wavelengths will coincide}
\opt{B}{The third order bright fringe of $\lambda_1$ will coincide with the fourth order bright fringe of $\lambda_2$}
\opt{C}{The third order dark fringe of $\lambda_2$ will coincide with fourth order dark fringe of $\lambda_1$}
\opt{D}{The fringes of wavelength $\lambda_1$ will be wider than the fringes of wavelength $\lambda_2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S1-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=multi, subtopic={YDSE}, answer={A,C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: YDSE, film or source shift changing fringe position | steps: path difference from slab or displaced source; central maximum shifts; fringe width; check | I: extra path from film and geometry together}]
In YDSE a screen is at a distance 80 cm from two narrow slits s$_1$ and s$_2$ which are 2 mm apart. Slit s$_1$ is covered by a transparent sheet of thickness 2.5 $\mu$m and slit s$_2$ is covered by another sheet of thickness 1.25 $\mu$m as shown.
\bfig{141.3}{SI07_p1_phy_s1_q05_1.png}
Both sheets are made of same material of refractive index 1.4. Water is also filled between slits and screen. Then [Wavelength of light in air = 5000\AA, Refractive index of water = 4/3]
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Central maxima is above the point C}
\opt{B}{Distance of central maxima is 0.015mm from C.}
\opt{C}{The resultant intensity at C is 75\% of maximum intensity}
\opt{D}{Fringe width is 0.15 mm.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S2-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={YDSE}, answer={2}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: YDSE, air layer in a hollow glass tube between slits | steps: optical path difference from refractive index changes; shift of fringes; count; evaluate | I: extra optical path from an enclosed layer}]
In a standard Young's double-slit experiment, a thin layer of air of thickness t$_2$ is enclosed in a hollow squarish transparent container of wall thickness t$_1$ as shown in figure.
\bfig{69.3}{SI07_p1_phy_s2_q05_1.png}
When it is placed in front of one slit, causes the shifting of central maxima by 4 fringe width, and when the entire setup is immersed in a liquid then it is observed that the central maxima is restored to the original position. Find the side length of container in $\mu$m.

[Wavelength of light in air = 500 nm, Refractive index of container = 1.5, Refractive index of liquid = 1.4]
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S3-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=numerical, subtopic={Interference}, answer={6.28 to 6.30}, answer_src=key, difficulty=7, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: sound source, two detectors path difference | steps: distance from source to detectors; path difference between D1 and D2; phase difference; intensity or wavelength asked | I: geometry gives the path difference}]

\begin{bankq}[id=SI07-P1-PHY-S3-Q05, source={Score-I - Test 07 (04 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=5, type=numerical, subtopic={Interference}, answer={5.00}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K1 S2 I2 C1 F1}, diff_note={concepts: thin film coating on diamond: thickness for minimum reflection | steps: reflection phase changes at both surfaces; condition 2 n t = (m + 1/2) lambda; minimum thickness; evaluate | I: phase changes at two interfaces both pi}]

\bfig{81.1}{SI07_p1_phy_s3_q05_1.png}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI08-P1-PHY-S1-Q04, source={Score-I - Test 08 (09 Feb 2022)}, paper=1, qno=4, type=single, subtopic={YDSE}, answer={B}, answer_src=key, difficulty=6, diff_parts={K2 S2 I2 C1 F0}, diff_note={concepts: intensity at a point, YDSE from central maximum value | steps: I = I0 cos^2(phi/2); phase from path difference; intensity at the given point; evaluate | I: phase from geometry of the screen point}]
In a YDSE apparatus, the intensity at the central maxima is 4 W/m$^2$. Both the slits are of equal width and the wavelength of the light used is 600 nm. An extremely thin glass plate of thickness 200 nm and refractive index 1.5 is placed in front of one of the slits and it is seen that the intensity at the centre of the screen (where earlier there was central maxima) is now 1.75 W/m$^2$. It is suspected that the glass plate absorbs some light. What is the new intensity at the central maxima ?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{3.00 W/m$^2$}
\opt{B}{2.25 W/m$^2$}
\opt{C}{3.60 W/m$^2$}
\opt{D}{2.40 W/m$^2$}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI12-P1-PHY-S1-Q08, source={Score-I - Test 12 (09 Mar 2022)}, paper=1, qno=8, type=multi, subtopic={Interference}, answer={C,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: interference of two virtual sources | steps: locate the two images; path difference at P; maxima condition for the options | I: images behave as two coherent sources}]
$M_1$ and $M_2$ are two plane mirror \& $S$ is monochromatic source. $AB$ is a `stop' which stops direct light to reach $CF$ and allows reflected light from $M_1$ and $M_2$ to reach $CF$. $P$ is a point on $CF$ such that $SP$ is parallel to $M_1$ \& $M_2$ and perpendicular to $CF$:
\bfig{131.7}{SI12_p1_phy_s1_q08_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{Circular fringes will be formed on $CF$}
\opt{B}{$P$ will be central maxima}
\opt{C}{$P$ will be a point of maxima if $\lambda=\dfrac{6d^2}{D}$}

\end{qoptions}

\opt{B}{500 nm}
\opt{C}{300 nm}
\opt{D}{100 nm}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI26-P1-PHY-S1-Q02, source={Score-I - Test 26 (18 Dec 2022)}, paper=1, qno=2, type=multi, subtopic={Polarization}, answer={B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=5, diff_parts={K1 S3 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: statements about polarisation of light | steps: reflected light from water is partially polarised; at Brewster angle reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular; Malus law; polaroid facts; check each}]
Mark the correct statements about polarisation of light.
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{If a polaroid is kept in front of you and rotated while looking at the light reflected from water or glass, you will notice that light gets bright and completely dark sequencially.}
\opt{B}{At Brewster's angle of incidence the plane of vibration of electric field vector of reflected light is perpendicular to plane of reflection}
\opt{C}{A polaroid consists of long chain molecules alinged in direction parallel to the axis of polaroid which absorb the electromagnetic energy of light.}
\opt{D}{If $\theta_1$ is the Brewster's angle for light reflected from the top of an interface between two substances and $\theta_2$ is the Brewster's angle for light reflected from below, then $\theta_1+\theta_2=90^\circ$.}

\begin{bankq}[id=SI26-P1-PHY-S1-Q03, source={Score-I - Test 26 (18 Dec 2022)}, paper=1, qno=3, type=multi, subtopic={Diffraction}, answer={A,B,D}, answer_src=key, difficulty=4, diff_parts={K2 S1 I1 C0 F1}, diff_note={concepts: Single slit diffraction, geometry of fringe positions | steps: dimensions of central fringe in single slit diffraction | central width 2 D lambda/W = 450 W gives W^2 relation with D = 18000 W; lambda/W ratio; position of second minimum; angular width; check each | I: use width of central maximum to fix the ratio of wavelength to slit width}]
In a single-slit diffraction pattern the central fringe is 450 times as wide as the slit. The screen is 18000 times farther from the slit than the slit is wide. The wave length of light is $\lambda$ and width of slit is `W'. [$\pi^2=10$]
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The ratio $\dfrac{W}{\lambda}$ is 80.}
\opt{B}{The distance of second minima from the point of maximum intensity is 450 W}
\opt{C}{The distance of second maxima from the point of maximum intensity is 450 W}
\opt{D}{If the angular position of the point where intensity is 0.9 times the maximum intensity is $\theta$, then $\sin\theta\approx\dfrac{1}{480}$ .}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}

\begin{bankpassage}[id=SA06-P1-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={Score Advanced - Test 06 (04 Sep 2021)}, questions={9-10}]
An electromagnetic wave can be represented by E = A sin (kx -- $\omega$t + $\phi$), where E is electric field associated with wave. According this equation, for any value of x, E remains sinusoidal for $-\infty$ $<$ t $<$ $\infty$. Obviously this corresponds to an idealised situation because radiation from ordinary source consists of finite size wavetrains. In general, electric field remains sinusoidal only for times of order $\tau_C$, which is called coherence time. In simpler language it means that for times of order $\tau_C$, a wave will have a definite phase. The finite value of coherence time could be due to many factors, for example if radiating atom undergoes collision with another atom then wave train undergoes an abrupt phase change or due to the fact that an atom responsible for emitting radiation has a finite life time in the energy level from which it drops to lower energy level, while radiating. Concept of coherence time can be easily understood using young's double slit experiment. Let interference pattern is observed around point P at time t, due to superposition of waves emanting from S$_1$ and S$_2$ at times t = $\dfrac{r_1}{c}$ and $\dfrac{r_2}{c}$ respectively, where r$_1$ and r$_2$ are the distance S$_1$P \& S$_2$P. Obviously if $\dfrac{r_2-r_1}{c}$ $<<$ $\tau_c$, \{where c = 3 $\times$ 10$^8$ m/s\} then, wavetrain arriving at point P from S$_1$ \& S$_2$ will have a definite phase relationship and an interference pattern of good contrast will be obtained.\par
\bfig{136.8}{SA06_p1_phy_s2_para9_10_1.png}
\end{bankpassage}

The film drains under gravity, being thicker at the bottom than at the top, where the thickness can be considered to be zero. The film is viewed, by reflection, with red and violet light at near normal incidence; the angle of incidence being exceedingly small. Interference results from light reflected from the outer surface and that emerging after reflection at the inner surface of the film. The first violet, wavelength 420 nm, constructive interference band is observed at a distance $x_v=3.0$ cm from the top edge of the film. The wavelength of the red light is 700 nm.
\bfig{55.6}{PS02_p1_phy_s1_q04_1.png}
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The thickness of the film at the lowest order constructive violet interference is 70 nm.}
\opt{B}{The film wedge angle $\phi$ is $2.33\times10^{-6}$ radian.}
\opt{C}{For the red light, the distance of lowest order constructive interference from the top of the film is 2.5 cm.}
\opt{D}{The soap film drains resulting in a decrease in wedge angle at a rate of $8\times10^{-5}$ rad/min. The initial speed of observed red interference fringes is 5.7 cm/s.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
\begin{bankpassage}[id=PS02-P1-PHY-S2-G9-10, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 02 (15 Oct 2023)}, questions={9-10}]
A colloid consists of particles of one type of substance dispersed in another substance. Suspensions of electrically charged microspheres (microscopic spheres, such as polystyrene) in a liquid such as water can form a colloidal crystal when the microspheres arrange themselves in a regular repeating pattern under the influence of the electrostatic force. Colloidal crystals can selectively manipulate different wavelengths of visible light. Just as we can study crystal-line solids by using Bragg reflection of x rays, we can study colloidal crystals through Bragg scattering of visible light from the regular arrangement of charged microspheres. Because the light is traveling through a liquid when it experiences the path differences that lead to constructive interference, it is the wavelength in the liquid that determines the angles at which Bragg reflections are seen. In one experiment, laser light with a wavelength in vacuum of 650 nm is passed through a sample of charged polystyrene spheres in water. A strong interference maximum is then observed when the incident and reflected beams make an angle of $39^\circ$ with the colloidal crystal planes.
\end{bankpassage}
\begin{bankq}[id=PS02-P1-PHY-S2-Q09, source={Pre-Score (2023-24) - Test 02 (15 Oct 2023)}, paper=1, qno=9, type=single, subtopic={Diffraction}, answer={D}, answer_src=key, working={Printed key.}, difficulty=3, diff_parts={K1 S2 I1 C0 F0}, diff_note={concepts: Bragg reflection of visible light from colloidal crystals | steps: Bragg condition needs wavelength comparable to lattice spacing; microsphere spacing is comparable to visible wavelength not atomic spacing; pick the reason | I: the lattice constant of a colloidal crystal is much larger than an atomic crystal}, group=PS02-P1-PHY-S2-G9-10]
Why is visible light, which has much longer wavelengths than x rays do, used for Bragg reflection experiments on colloidal crystals?
\begin{qoptions}
\opt{A}{The microspheres are suspended in a liquid, and it is more difficult for x rays to penetrate liquid than it is for visible light.}
\opt{B}{The irregular spacing of the microspheres allows the longer wavelength visible light to produce more destructive interference than can x rays.}
\opt{C}{The microspheres are much larger than atoms in a crystalline solid, and in order to get interference maxima at reasonably large angles, the wavelength must be much longer than the size of the individual scatterers.}
\opt{D}{The microspheres are spaced more widely than atoms in a crystalline solid, and in order to get interference maxima at reasonably large angles, the wavelength must be comparable to the spacing between scattering planes.}
\end{qoptions}
\end{bankq}
